sections.explanation: Changing the subject expresses one symbol in terms of the others. The operations are the same as equation solving, but a divisor may now be a parameter that could equal zero. Record the non-zero condition before division and examine the exceptional case in the original relation. A formula valid when a ≠ 0 is not a solution of the a = 0 case.
sections.worked: From y = ax + b, subtract b: y − b = ax. If a ≠ 0, x = (y − b)/a. If a = 0, the original says y = b: every x works when y = b, and no x works when y ≠ b.
tasks: Make t the subject of s = s₀ + vt, with restriction.
Make b the subject of y = ax + b.
Make x the subject of p = qx − r, with restriction.
For y = ax + b, classify a = 0, y = 3, b = 3 and a = 0, y = 4, b = 3.
feedback: b = y − ax; no division restriction is introduced.
Every x in the first case; no x in the second.

sections.explanation: If the target appears in several terms, collect and factor it before dividing. Check every denominator in the original formula as well as any new divisor. Some operations are not reversible: squaring equal numbers preserves equality, but equal squares do not imply equal originals. Therefore a candidate obtained through an irreversible step must be checked in the original statement. We are learning this safeguard, not beginning a general method for nonlinear equations.
sections.worked: From p = ax + bx, factor: p = (a + b)x. Thus x = p/(a + b) if a + b ≠ 0. When a + b = 0, the relation requires p = 0. Separately, x = −3 implies x² = 9, but the squared statement also admits x = 3, which fails the original.
tasks: Make x the subject of p = ax + c − bx.
State the exceptional cases when a = b in that relation.
Make v the subject of t = d/v, retaining the original restriction and any new one.
Show explicitly that x = 3 passes x² = 9 but fails x = −3.
Explain why substituting into the final transformed equation alone can miss an added candidate.
feedback: If p = c every x works; otherwise none.
v = d/t for t ≠ 0, with v ≠ 0 from the original; the t = 0 case must be considered separately (then d = 0 and any non-zero v works).
The transformed equation may have a larger solution set than the original.

sections.explanation: Translate the restriction into a guard before evaluating a rearranged formula. The else branch need not solve every exceptional case automatically; it can explain that a separate analysis is required. Compare the recovered value with the original relation by substituting it back. Small exact integer examples make the logic clear without introducing rounding tolerances yet.
sections.worked: For y = 11, a = 2, b = 3, the recovered x is 4. Substitution gives 2 × 4 + 3 = 11. At a = 0 the program should report the exceptional case rather than divide.
tasks: Run the example, then change a to 0 and predict the branch.
For a = 0, analyse y = 3 and y = 11 by hand with b = 3.
Use y = −5, a = −2, b = 3; predict x before running.
Explain what the printed reconstructed y checks and what it does not check.
feedback: 4.0 and 11.0, then a message when a = 0.
All x for y = 3; none for y = 11.
It checks this numerical substitution; it does not establish that the physical calibration model is appropriate.
sections.code:
y = 11
a = 2
b = 3
if a != 0:
    x = (y - b) / a
    print(x)
    print(a * x + b)
else:
    print("Zero scale: analyse y = b separately")

sections.explanation: A useful inverse formula must retain a physical interpretation. In s = s₀ + vt, the v = 0 case describes a stationary object. If the target coordinate equals s₀ it is occupied throughout the modelled interval; otherwise it is never reached. This is not merely a software error. Restrictions often encode meaningful special cases.
sections.worked: For s₀ = 5 m and v = 0, the question “when is s = 5 m?” has every time in the model interval as an answer. The question “when is s = 8 m?” has no answer. The quotient (s − 5)/0 must not be used.
tasks: Explain the two stationary cases in your own words.
For s = 17 m, s₀ = 5 m, v = 3 m/s, calculate and check t.
For the same target with v = −3 m/s, interpret the candidate when only t ≥ 0 is allowed.
State why “undefined quotient” alone is an incomplete physical explanation.
feedback: At the starting coordinate all model times qualify; at another coordinate none do.
t = −4 s, so no future arrival within the specified model.
The original equation can still determine whether there are no solutions or many, even though the rearranged quotient is unavailable.

tasks: Make x the subject of q=cx −d.
When c=0, classify q=−d and q≠−d.
feedback: Every x in the first case; no x in the second.
